entry: Physical law relating the thermal radiation of a black body to its temperature. States that the total energy radiated per unit surface area per unit time by a black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its temperature. The constant of proportionality, σ, is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant. For other surfaces the radiant exitance is M = εσT⁴, where ε is the emissivity, generally between zero and one. Josef Stefan derived the relationship empirically, and [[Ludwig Boltzmann]] derived the law theoretically.

Serbian king (1331–1355) and emperor of the Serbs, Greeks, Bulgarians and Albanians (1346–1355). Also called Dušan the Mighty, he conquered a large part of Southeast Europe. Under him [[Serbia]] was the most powerful state in Southeast Europe, stretching from the [[Danube]] in the north to the Gulf of Corinth in the south, with its capital at [[Skopje]]. He enacted the constitution of the Serbian Empire, known as Dušan's Code, perhaps the most important literary work of medieval Serbia. He raised the Serbian Church from an archbishopric to a patriarchate and completed the Visoki Dečani Monastery, now a [[UNESCO]] site. He sought an alliance with Venice against the advancing Ottoman Turks, but after his death the Serbian Empire weakened and was divided into independent states. His remains were later moved to the Church of Saint Mark in [[Belgrade]].

German former professional tennis player. She was ranked world No. 1 by the Women's Tennis Association for a record 377 weeks and won 22 major women's singles titles. She is the only player to have won each major singles tournament at least four times, a quadruple career [[Grand Slam (tennis)|Grand Slam]]. In 1988 she became the first tennis player to achieve the Golden Slam, winning all four major titles and the Olympic gold medal in the same calendar year. After injuries and the rise of rivals such as [[Monica Seles]], she won her 22nd and final major at the 1999 French Open and retired that year, aged 30. Her versatile game, built on a powerful forehand and baseline play, is credited with developing the style that dominates today's game. She has been married to [[Andre Agassi]] since 2001.

Genus of extinct, four-legged, herbivorous armored dinosaurs from the Late Jurassic. Its name means "roof-lizard." It had kite-shaped upright plates along its back and spikes on its tail, and is one of the most recognizable kinds of dinosaurs. Fossils have been found in the western United States and in [[Portugal]], dating to between 155 and 145 million years ago, and fossils of over 80 individuals have been found. It lived alongside [[Diplodocus]] and [[Allosaurus]], which may have preyed on it. The spiked tail was most likely used for defense, while the plates may have been used mainly for display and secondarily for thermoregulation. The largest specimens of *Stegosaurus ungulatus* measured about 9 m (30 ft) long. Othniel Charles Marsh first identified its remains during the "Bone Wars."

[[Black hole]] formed by the gravitational collapse of a star. Stellar black holes have masses ranging from about five to several tens of [[Solar mass|solar masses]]. They can be the remnants of [[Supernova|supernova]] explosions, although other formation mechanisms may operate. A black hole has only three fundamental properties: mass, electric charge and [[Angular momentum|angular momentum]], and the angular momentum of a stellar black hole comes from the star or objects that produced it. In close binary systems, matter transferred from a companion star heats up and radiates in X-rays, making the black hole observable. In September 2015 a rotating black hole of 62±4 solar masses was discovered through [[Gravitational wave|gravitational waves]] as it formed in the merger of two smaller black holes.

Scheme for grouping stars by the features of their spectra. Light from a star is split by a [[Prism (optics)|prism]] or [[Diffraction grating|diffraction grating]] into a spectrum whose lines show which chemical elements or [[Molecule|molecules]] are present; their strength mainly reflects the temperature of the photosphere. Most stars are classified by the Morgan–Keenan (MK) system, which uses the letters O, B, A, F, G, K and M from hottest to coolest, each subdivided by a digit from 0 (hottest) to 9 (coolest). Luminosity classes in [[Roman numerals]] distinguish giants from dwarfs, running from class 0 or Ia+ for hypergiants to class V for main-sequence stars. The [[Sun]] is classed G2V, indicating a main-sequence star with a surface temperature of about 5,800 K. The spectral class comes from the older Harvard system, which Annie Jump Cannon developed by simplifying an alphabetical scheme.

Process by which a star changes over the course of time. Depending on mass, a star's lifetime ranges from a few million years for the most massive to trillions of years for the least massive. Stars form from collapsing clouds of gas and dust, settle into a [[Main sequence|main-sequence]] state, and fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores. Stars like the [[Sun]] later swell into [[Red giant|red giants]], and when their fuel is exhausted their cores become [[White dwarf|white dwarfs]] while the outer layers are expelled as a planetary nebula. Stars with around ten or more times the mass of the Sun can explode as [[Supernova|supernovae]], leaving a [[Neutron star]] or a [[Black hole]]. Because most changes are too slow to observe in a single star, astrophysicists study many stars at different stages and simulate stellar structure with computer models.

Study of the observed motions of stars through space. It measures stellar velocities in the [[Milky Way]] and its satellites, and the internal kinematics of more distant [[Galaxy|galaxies]]. The radial velocity of a star is measured from the shift of its spectrum caused by the [[Doppler effect]], while its proper motion must be found from a series of positional measurements against distant objects. Once distance is known, through means such as [[Parallax]], the space velocity can be computed relative to the local standard of rest. Measured velocities in the inner regions of galaxies provide evidence that many host [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black holes]] at their centers, and velocities of globular clusters in galactic halos provide evidence for [[Dark matter]]. Hypervelocity stars escaping the Milky Way are interpreted as the result of encounters with the supermassive black hole at the [[Galactic Center]].

Magnetic field generated by the motion of conductive [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]] inside a star. Convection moves this plasma, and a localized field rises until it reaches the photosphere, creating starspots on the surface and related coronal loops. According to solar dynamo theory, the convective zone acts as a dynamo: circulation destroys the primordial field and generates a dipolar field, which differential rotation winds into toroidal flux ropes that emerge at the surface. The [[Sun]]'s major magnetic component reverses direction every 11 years, so the full period is about 22 years. Stellar fields are measured with the Zeeman effect, in which a magnetic field splits spectral lines into closely spaced lines and polarizes the light according to the field's orientation.

Model describing the internal structure of a star and predicting its luminosity, color and future evolution. Different classes and ages of stars have different internal structures, reflecting their composition and energy transport mechanisms. Heat moves outward mainly by [[Convection|convection]] and radiative transfer. Stars of 0.3–1.5 solar masses, including the [[Sun]], fuse hydrogen mainly through proton–proton chains, so their cores are radiative and their outer envelopes convective. In stars above about 1.5 solar masses the CNO cycle dominates, which makes the core convective and the envelope radiative. The lowest-mass main-sequence stars convect throughout. The simplest commonly used model assumes a steady, spherically symmetric star described by four first-order differential equations, including the condition of [[Hydrostatic equilibrium|hydrostatic equilibrium]].

Extinct [[Sirenia|sirenian]] mammal (*Hydrodamalis gigas*). Described by Georg Wilhelm Steller in 1741, it was then found only around the Commander Islands in the [[Bering Sea]]. Steller first encountered it when shipwrecked on Bering Island during [[Vitus Bering]]'s Great Northern Expedition. This slow-moving, easily caught animal was hunted into extinction within 27 years of its discovery, for its meat, fat and hide. Adults are estimated to have weighed 8–10 t and reached lengths up to 9 m (30 ft). It fed mainly on [[Kelp|kelp]] and had no true teeth.

Unspecialized [[Cell (biology)|cell]] that can change into various specialized cell types and proliferate. Stem cells can produce more of the same stem cell indefinitely, distinguishing them from progenitor cells, which cannot divide indefinitely. In [[Mammal|mammals]], the inner cell mass of the blastocyst, around days 5–14 of development, can differentiate into all of the body's cell types. Adult stem cells in niches such as bone marrow replenish rapidly lost cell types and are multipotent or unipotent. As of 2016, the only established medical therapy using stem cells was hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, first performed in 1958. Since 1998 human embryonic stem cells have been cultured, a process considered controversial because it typically destroys the [[Embryo]]. In 2006 a Japanese team led by Shinya Yamanaka converted mature body cells into induced pluripotent stem cells.

French writer, pen name of Marie-Henri Beyle. Best known for the novels *Le Rouge et le Noir* (1830) and *La Chartreuse de Parme* (1839), he is considered one of the early and foremost practitioners of realism, and was admired for his acute analysis of his characters' psychology. His work *De l'amour* on passionate love introduced the concept of crystallization; it was mostly ignored on publication but was later praised as one of the first modern attempts to understand love. He served as an assistant war commissioner in the administration of the Kingdom of Westphalia, a client state of [[Napoleon]], and took part in the 1812 invasion of Russia. He settled in [[Milan]] for several years, and in 1830 he was appointed French consul at Trieste and Civitavecchia.

Family in which at least one parent has children who are not biologically related to their spouse. Also called a bonus family, it is "simple" if only one partner has a prior child and the couple has none together, or "complex" or "blended" if both partners have children from other relationships. The prefix *step-* appears in Old English words for [[Orphan|orphan]] and first denoted a connection formed by a widowed parent's remarriage. A stepparent is the spouse of a child's parent who is not the biological parent. Stepparents often face significant difficulties with the biological parent of the same gender, who may fear being replaced in the child's mind. In most of the United States a stepparent is a "legal stranger" with no legal right to the child, however involved they are in the child's life.

Hungarian nobleman, king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania (1576–1586). He was voivode of [[Transylvania]] from 1571 and defeated a rival, Gáspár Bekes, to establish his position there. In 1576 he married Queen Anna Jagiellon and was elected king of Poland, working closely with Chancellor Jan Zamoyski. His first years were devoted to establishing his power and quelling rebellions, most notably the [[Gdańsk]] rebellion. His signal achievement was a campaign in Livonia against Russia, which repulsed a Russian invasion of the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]] borderlands and produced the favorable Peace of Jam Zapolski. He is considered one of the most successful kings in Polish and Lithuanian history, particularly in military affairs, although he reigned for only a decade.

American comedian, writer and television host. He hosted the Comedy Central news satire *The Colbert Report* from 2005 to 2014 and the [[CBS]] late-night show *The Late Show with Stephen Colbert* from 2015 to 2026. His satirical persona parodied conservative pundits and introduced the word truthiness, named Word of the Year by the American Dialect Society and Merriam-Webster. He has won eleven Primetime Emmy Awards, two [[Grammy Awards]] and three Peabody Awards. In 2011 he started the satirical Colbert Super PAC, which was credited with raising awareness of campaign finance issues.

American basketball player for the Golden State Warriors. Widely regarded as the greatest shooter in [[Basketball|basketball]] history, he is credited with popularizing the three-point shot. He won four [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] championships and two league MVP awards, and in 2022 became the NBA's all-time leader in three-pointers made. He set the NCAA single-season record for three-pointers made (162) as a sophomore at Davidson College. He also won two FIBA World Cup gold medals and a gold medal at the 2024 Summer Olympics with the United States national team.

English actor, comedian and writer. He began on the sketch series *Alfresco* and the sitcom *Blackadder* before forming the comedy duo Fry and Laurie with [[Hugh Laurie]]. He hosted the panel show *QI* from 2003 to 2016 and was nominated for a Golden Globe for playing [[Oscar Wilde]] in *Wilde* (1997). He has written four novels and three autobiographies, and narrated the audiobooks of all seven [[Harry Potter]] novels. He has been president of the mental health charity Mind since 2011 and was knighted in 2025 for services to mental health awareness, the environment and charity.

English theoretical physicist and cosmologist. He collaborated with Roger Penrose on singularity theorems in [[General relativity|general relativity]] and predicted that [[Black hole|black holes]] emit radiation, now called [[Hawking radiation]]. Initially controversial, the prediction was widely accepted as a major breakthrough by the late 1970s. He was the first to set out a theory of cosmology combining general relativity and [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. Diagnosed with motor neurone disease in 1963, he lost the use of his speech and later communicated through a speech-generating device, eventually using a single cheek muscle. He was Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the [[University of Cambridge|University of Cambridge]] from 1979 to 2009. His book *A Brief History of Time* appeared on the *Sunday Times* bestseller list for a record 237 weeks.

First king of Hungary (1000 or 1001–1038) and Catholic saint. Born Vajk, he succeeded his father as grand prince in 997 and defeated his relative Koppány, who had large numbers of pagan warriors behind him, with the help of foreign knights. He was crowned with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II. In a series of wars he unified the Carpathian Basin, and he forced the invading troops of Conrad II, Holy Roman Emperor, to withdraw in 1030. He established at least one archbishopric and six bishoprics, and organized local government into counties run by royal officials. Hungary enjoyed lasting peace under his rule and became a preferred route for pilgrims and merchants between [[Western Europe]] and [[Constantinople]]. He was canonized in 1083, and his feast day, celebrated on 20 August, is a public holiday known as State Foundation Day.

American [[Paleontology|paleontologist]], evolutionary biologist and historian of science. With Niles Eldredge he developed the theory of punctuated equilibrium in 1972, holding that most evolution consists of long periods of stability interrupted by swift bursts of branching speciation, in contrast to phyletic gradualism. He taught mostly at [[Harvard University]] and worked at the [[American Museum of Natural History]] in New York. He opposed the overemphasis on [[Natural selection|natural selection]] and criticized biological determinism in sociobiology and [[Evolutionary psychology|evolutionary psychology]]. As a public advocate for science, he campaigned against creationism and argued that science and religion are distinct fields, or "non-overlapping magisteria." His essays in *Natural History* magazine made him widely known, and in 2000 the U.S. Library of Congress named him a "Living Legend."

American author of [[Horror fiction|horror]], dubbed the "King of Horror." His debut, *Carrie* (1974), established him in horror, and *Different Seasons* (1982), a collection of four novellas, was his first major departure from the genre. He has written approximately 200 short stories and has also explored suspense, crime, science fiction, [[Fantasy|fantasy]] and mystery. Adaptations of his fiction include *The Shining* (1980), *Stand by Me* (1986), *Misery* (1990), *The Shawshank Redemption* (1994) and *The Green Mile* (1999). He has also published as Richard Bachman and co-written works with Peter Straub and his sons Joe Hill and Owen King. His nonfiction includes *Danse Macabre* (1981) and *On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft* (2000). He received the 2003 Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters and the 2014 National Medal of Arts.

American composer and lyricist of musical [[Theatre|theater]]. He is credited with reinventing the American musical. He wrote lyrics for [[West Side Story]] (1957) and *Gypsy* (1959) before writing both music and lyrics. Five of his works won the Tony Award for Best Musical, including *Company* (1970) and *Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street* (1979). *Sunday in the Park with George* (1984) won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. He won eight Tony Awards and eight [[Grammy Awards]], and an Academy Award for Best Original Song for "Sooner or Later" from *Dick Tracy* (1990).

Voivode of [[Moldavia]] (1457–1504) and national hero of [[Romania]] and [[Moldova]]. He took the throne after his victory at the Battle of Orbic, with support from his cousin [[Vlad the Impaler]]. He stopped paying tribute to the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottomans]] in 1473 and defeated a large Ottoman army at the Battle of Vaslui in 1475, earning the title *Athleta Christi* ("Champion of Christ") from Pope Sixtus IV. The following year Mehmed II routed him at Valea Albă, and his efforts to recapture the ports of Chilia and Cetatea Albă ended in failure. From 1486 he again paid a yearly tribute to the Ottomans. He restored old fortresses and built new ones, and dozens of stone churches and monasteries were built during his reign, contributing to a distinct Moldavian architectural style. The Romanian Orthodox Church canonized him in 1992.

Ecoregion of plain grasslands without closed forests except near rivers and lakes. Steppes are usually covered with grass and shrubs, depending on season and latitude, and have a semi-arid or continental climate. Temperatures can reach 45 °C (115 °F) in summer and fall to −55 °C (−65 °F) in winter. Steppes average 250–500 mm (10–20 in) of precipitation a year. The world's largest steppe region, often called the Great Steppe, runs across [[Eastern Europe]] and [[Central Asia]] from [[Ukraine]] to the Altai and Tian Shan ranges. The [[Eurasian Steppe]] had a significant role in the spread of the horse, the wheel and [[Indo-European languages]]. In North America, the shortgrass prairie is the westernmost part of the [[Great Plains]].
